title: Counterfactual-sensitivity scoring & judge confidence harmonization for config rollouts
creator: Asha Mehta
description:
Problem: Current eval signal relies on static rubric weights and single-stage LLM-as-judge votes which miss subtle distributional shifts introduced by config or model changes (quantization profiles, batching, KV cache policies, temperature). We see noisy judge confidence and cohort-specific sensitivity that can mask small-but-actionable regressions during canary rollouts.

Proposal: Build a counterfactual-sensitivity scoring layer plus judge confidence harmonization pipeline. Key pieces: (1) Counterfactual-sensitivity scoring (CSS) — compute per-example sensitivity by simulating small perturbations to model/config (e.g., +5% temp, alternative quantization path) and measuring sign/score change in outputs; aggregate into a sensitivity signal that highlights examples likely to flip under config deltas. (2) Judge confidence harmonization — train a lightweight meta-judge that rescales judge logits across judge runs using temperature-aware calibration and Bayesian shrinkage so confidence differences are comparable across judges and model variants. (3) Cohort reweighting using noise-aware importance weights — reweight eval cohorts by their CSS score and by historical judge variance so the rollout metric focuses on fragile cohorts. (4) Integration: wire CSS + harmonized judge confidence into the rollout gating dashboard, add early-warning alert rules (e.g., precision-adjusted regression probability > 0.95), and surface per-cohort counterfactual diffs in the Console eval view.

Trade-offs: CSS requires running small perturbation experiments that increase eval compute ~1.4x per config variant; harmonization requires collecting judge logits and building a small calibration service. Benefit is earlier detection of regressions that affect high-sensitivity cohorts, and reduced false positives from judge confidence drift.

Deliverables: proposal doc, calibration service prototype, evaluation harness changes (cohort weighting + CSS), Console dashboard mock, rollout gating rule definitions, and an ops runbook for compute cost and alert tuning.

Links: proposal doc (https://docs.google.com/document/d/1Counterfactual-Scoring-Proposal), prototype notebook (https://github.com/redwood-inference/evals/tree/main/css-proto), related design notes (https://drive.google.com/file/d/design-notes-css.pdf).
acceptance_criteria: 1) Prototype computes CSS at scale on our 10k benchmark set and returns per-example sensitivity scores with <5% missing rate. 2) Meta-judge calibration reduces expected calibration error (ECE) of judge probabilities by >=30% versus raw judge logits on validation split. 3) Cohort-weighted rollout metric flags at least 80% of historical regressions (post-hoc validation) while keeping false positive rate <= 5%. 4) Console surfaces per-cohort counterfactual diffs and a gating flag that can block a canary rollout in the UI. 5) Runbook documents compute cost impact and tuning knobs.
metrics: CSS: mean sensitivity (fraction of perturbations that change output)
Judge ECE before and after harmonization
notes: We should avoid overfitting the meta-judge to current judges; prefer a holdout and periodic re-calibration schedule (monthly).
Consider running CSS only on golden prompt subsets and high-traffic cohorts to reduce compute cost initially.
Engineering estimates show ~1.4x eval time for single additional perturbation type; if we include two perturbation axes compute rises ~2.1x.
Potential downstream: expose CSS as an opt-in signal to Dedicated customers who run private evals.
Align with privacy: ensure judge logits stored with access controls; do not include raw customer content in shared datasets.
